facts.name: Daffodil
facts.notes: Plant bulbs in October, 6 to 8 inches deep, in clumps of 5 to 8. Comes back and spreads for years, and deer and squirrels leave it alone. Let the leaves yellow before cutting them back.

sources.title: English Gardens (Detroit-area garden centers): Fall is for planting
sources.note: Michigan garden center; names tulips and daffodils among the fall bulbs to plant.

sources.title: Mississippi State Extension: Don't Touch the Daffodils
sources.note: Leave bulb leaves untouched for at least six weeks after they start to look dried up.

sources.title: Purdue Extension (Marion County): Gardening with Bulbs
sources.note: Daffodils naturalize and are squirrel and deer resistant; hybrid tulips are 'like candy to squirrels and deer'; squirrels don't eat alliums; interplant bulbs with later perennials that hide the ripening leaves; plant from mid-October.

sources.title: UW-Madison Extension: Plant Bulbs Now for Spring Color
sources.note: Plant large bulbs 6 to 8 in deep in clumps of 5 to 8; squirrels are less likely to dig daffodils than tulips.

sources.title: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox: Daffodils
sources.note: Daffodils are deer and rabbit resistant and toxic to cats, dogs and horses (bulbs most of all).

sources.title: ASPCA: Daffodil, Tulip and Onion plant pages
sources.note: Daffodil (Narcissus), tulip (Tulipa) and onion (Allium) are all listed as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: Upper Midwest Home Garden Care Calendar
sources.note: Divide bearded iris late July to early August and peonies from late August; plant spring bulbs from September to mid-November.

companions.why: Purdue Extension: interplant daffodils with late-emerging, sturdy perennials such as hosta, grasses or daylilies.
